title: Sugar: It Powers the Earth
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant cover sugar: its origins in New Guinea and Polynesia, spread through India, Persia, and the Crusades to Europe and the Caribbean via Columbus, its ties to slavery, the Venetian sugar trade and 1319 shipment to England, the Reformation and the rise of tea with sugar in Britain, the sugar beet and Napoleonic-era blockades, how sugarcane and sugar beets are processed (centrifuge, mother liquor, molasses, bagasse), sugar dust explosions, types of sugar (sucrose, glucose, fructose, lactose, xylitol, castor and preserving sugar), high fructose corn syrup and metabolic effects, sugar and tooth decay, diabetes and insulin resistance, sugar-based ethanol in Brazil, and microbial fuel cells. The episode ends with a listener mail rebutting a creationist's views on micro and macro evolution.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with chatter about sweet terms of endearment, a Simpsons bit, and a teaser about an upcoming table reading.

segments.title: Origins and spread of sugar
segments.summary: Sugar is traced from New Guinea and Polynesia through Indonesia and India, spreading via trade routes, Persians, the Crusades, and Columbus's sugarcane to the Caribbean and New World, tied to slavery.

segments.title: Sugar as luxury and the Venetian trade
segments.summary: Sugar was a royal luxury; Venice refined it and shipped fifty tons to England in 1319. The Reformation and wider availability made sugar accessible to the public, boosting tea drinking in Britain.

segments.title: Napoleonic blockades and sugar beets
segments.summary: Naval blockades during European wars led to the sugar beet becoming a source of sugar; beets yield about seventeen percent sugar versus about ten for cane.

segments.title: Sugar production process
segments.summary: Describes how sugar beets and sugarcane are sliced or pulverized, boiled into juice, filtered, centrifuged into crystals, and leave mother liquor. Sugar dust can seed crystallization and has caused explosions at a refinery.

segments.title: Byproducts and environmental impact
segments.summary: Molasses, rum, and bagasse are byproducts; bagasse powers refineries as fuel. Sugar production raises deforestation and worker concerns.

segments.title: Message break
segments.summary: Short message break before the discussion of sugar types.

segments.title: Types of sugar
segments.summary: Covers sucrose, glucose, fructose, lactose, xylose, xylitol and other sugar alcohols, and granulations such as icing, castor, granulated, and preserving sugar; preserving properties of sugar.

segments.title: High fructose corn syrup
segments.summary: High fructose corn syrup is compared with sucrose; fructose is processed by the liver and may be converted to fat more readily. Added sugars are debated, with US government guidance focusing on total added sugar.

segments.title: Sugar, teeth, diabetes, and metabolic syndrome
segments.summary: Sugar feeds bacteria like Streptococcus mutans that produce lactic acid and cause cavities. Excess sugar leads to insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome, heart disease, and type two diabetes.

segments.title: Sugar as fuel
segments.summary: Brazil ran largely on sugarcane ethanol, which was later outcompeted by cheap gasoline; sugar fuel competes with food and raises prices. Microbial fuel cells use sugar-eating microbes to generate electricity.

segments.title: Listener mail on creationism and evolution
segments.summary: A listener rebuttal explains that micro and macro evolution describe the same natural selection process on different timescales, responding to an earlier creationist listener email.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to contribute via Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website.
